title: The women who paid (Luke 8:1–3)
hookLine: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others funded his work

lines: WHO ELSE IS ON THE ROAD.
cards: Somebody has to pay for the bread. Thirteen men walking from village to village don't eat on good intentions. Someone buys the food, finds the beds, mends the sandals.
Matthew and Mark never say who. Luke does, in three short verses that are easy to read straight past. Jesus went through every city and village, preaching, "and the twelve were with him."
Then Luke names who else is on the road. Women, several named and many more not. And he tells us exactly what they were doing.

teach.h: OF THEIR SUBSTANCE: THEIR OWN MONEY.
teach.b: In the King James words: "And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils, And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance."
Of their substance means out of their own money and goods. These women were funding the work.

teach.h: MARY MAGDALENE: SEVEN DEMONS, NOT A PAST.
teach.b: Mary, from Magdala, a fishing town on the lake, healed of seven demons. That's all Luke says about her past.
Nothing about her being a prostitute; that idea came centuries later, when a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century merged her with yesterday's unnamed woman.
Eastern churches never made that link, and in modern times Catholic teaching has also set it aside.
Joanna was the wife of Chuza, who managed the household of Herod Antipas, the ruler who imprisoned John the Baptist. So money from inside that palace was quietly feeding Jesus' work.

And Susanna, mentioned here and nowhere else in the New Testament. One verse, and she's remembered for two thousand years. The word for ministered is diakoneo, to serve, to provide, the root of the word deacon.
And when the men scatter at the end of the Gospel, these women are still there.
Luke names Mary Magdalene and Joanna among the women at the empty tomb, the first to hear that he is risen.

teach.h: MANY OTHERS, WHICH MINISTERED UNTO HIM OF THEIR SUBSTANCE.
teach.b: The ones who paid for the road were the first witnesses at its end.

how: Many churches honor Mary Magdalene with a feast on July 22, and Orthodox Christians remember her among the Myrrh-bearing Women, who went to the tomb with spices.

games.q: you're Joanna. your husband runs Herod's household, the court that imprisoned John. a teacher has healed you. what do you do?
o: keep your head down; it's too risky.
travel with him and help pay for the work from your own means.
send a thank-you gift and stay at court.
games.why: Joanna travels with Jesus and supports him from her own means, and she's there at the empty tomb.

practice: Think about the work you're part of, a family, a team, a church, a household, and look for the people at the edges of the picture: who keeps the calendar, pays the bill without saying so, stays late to clean up.
Let one face come clearly, and picture what would fall apart if they stopped. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name; if you don't, simply hold them in gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Diakoneo, Greek for serving, providing for, the root of the word deacon: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others, who supported Jesus' work from their own means and were first at the empty tomb.

orig.note: Greek: they were serving, providing for. from diakoneo, the root of deacon.

carryVoice: Your line: the women paid. Quiet support is real work, and Luke wrote their names down. That's day five hundred thirty.
